idiom_name: count embedded in the body: handle copy increments, handle release decrements, zero destroys
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the shared body a count field initialised to 1 at its single creation point; give the handle - the small value users copy and pass around - a copy operation that increments and a destruction path that decrements and destroys the body exactly once when the count reaches zero. Keep exactly one count per body: handles are only ever created from an existing handle or from the creation function, never from an arbitrary pointer. Choose the counter policy deliberately - a plain integer while the object is guaranteed to stay on one thread, atomic or externally synchronised operations once handles can migrate - and make the release hook non-throwing and idempotent. Where the body already carries a count (COM IUnknown, Core Foundation, GObject, kernel krefs), do not add a second one: forward the handle's increment and release to the existing protocol.
code_sketch:
body = create(); body.count = 1            # single creation point
handle.copy():    body.count += 1
handle.release(): if --body.count == 0 { destroy(body) }
send(handle)      # receiver owns one count and must release it
# foreign counted object: ref = add_ref(obj); ...; release_ref(obj)
pitfalls: Two independent counts for one body (a handle built from a raw pointer that is also owned elsewhere) destroy it twice.
Cycles keep the body alive forever: counting is not collection.
A shared count without atomic operations or an external lock is a data race as soon as a handle crosses a thread.
ABA corruption: in free-list or lock-free implementations a location reused after deletion can be reallocated with a new body but the old count still visible, causing premature or delayed deletion.

Speculative execution and memory-reordering around atomic increments: a compiler or CPU may reorder the increment before a prior write that establishes the body validity, causing the count to be incremented on already-freed storage.

Custom deleters and std::destroying_delete interfere with the release hook: if the deleter runs before the count reaches zero (e.g. std::unique_ptr with a converting constructor), the body is freed without the intrusive decrement path being taken.
Object resurrection: a finalizer or pthread destructor can re-register a pointer to the object, bringing the count back above zero after it reached zero, leaking the object permanently.
Mixing intrusive_ptr (Boost) with shared_ptr for the same body: both think they own the count and both decrement on destruction, causing a double-decrement and undefined behavior.
Branching on use_count() or ref_count() under concurrency: the value is stale the instant it is read; a thread that observes count > 1 may find count == 1 by the time it acts.
Adopting a borrowed raw pointer as an owned handle: the caller retains ownership and releases the body while the intrusive handle still holds a count, causing use-after-free.
